newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Belarus pact latest move for newly active Yeltsin.
newsitem.headline: Belarus pact latest move for newly active Yeltsin.

text.p: Less than two months ago, Boris Yeltsin was being widely written off as history, his political career finally cut short by pneumonia on top of major heart surgery.

Since then he has revamped the Russian government, installing radical market reformers in top posts, delivered a 25-minute state-of-the-nation speech, and held a gruelling summit with a wheelchair-bound U.S. President Bill Clinton.

Then on Wednesday Yeltsin manifested his trademark political intuition and signed an audacious pact for a union between Russia and Belarus which suited -- at least in part -- all the parties involved.
As so often before, Yeltsin has bounced back with a vengeance.

Although he is much thinner than during his energetic campaign for reelection in the first half of last year, Yeltsin's resurgence suggests his four-year second presidential term is finally under way.

"They should know I am a fighter and I remain a fighter," Yeltsin warned his political foes in a rare walkabout outside the Kremlin on February 23. "They shouldn't attack me too hard because I can hit back."
The 66-year-old president had effectively been out of politics since his election victory last July. He underwent a quintuple heart bypass in November and was laid low by pneumonia in early January.
Now he has stunned friend and foe alike by returning to the Kremlin and reasserting his authority with unexpected vigour and the determination of old.
He announced his return by making a government reshuffle led by young reformers, warning opponents he will get tough if they try to block his reforms.

"I want to pass on to my successor a country with a dynamically growing economy, an effective and fair social protection system, a country whose people look to the future with confidence," he told parliament on March 6.
Both this state-of-the-nation speech and his Helsinki meeting with Clinton on March 19 and 20 showed his renewed stamina and ability to rule.
The Union Treaty was clearly a last-minute compromise with Belarus leader Alexander Lukashenko.

While satisfying broad public nostalgia for the former Soviet Union, Yeltsin also took into consideration the concerns of liberals at home that a hasty union might be too costly for Russia's economy and give a politial step up to Lukashenko.
Yeltsin's health problems are not surprising after a roller-coaster career in which he has fought many battles, taken repeated risks and handled problems on a huge scale.

He rose as a Communist Party official in the Soviet Union, but then became leader of the first legal opposition in the communist superpower, crushed the party and played a pivotal role in destroying the Soviet Union.

Elected Russia's president in 1991, he launched market reforms and helped keep relations with the United States and other Western countries on track, particularly at the time of the Soviet Union's collapse in December 1991.

Ties have since cooled and were not helped by the 20-month armed conflict in the breakaway Chechnya region which Yeltsin launched in 1994. Yeltsin's political problems after the Chechnya conflict erupted were compounded by two mild heart attacks in 1995 which put him out of action for months.
His popularity was just a little above zero by the start of 1996 but he pulled out all the stops to fight off communist challenger Gennady Zyuganov to secure a new term on July 3.
He criss-crossed the vast country, keeping to a punishing schedule and adding flourishes such as swinging on a swing and dancing the twist at a pop concert.
Gone was the halting walk, the slurred speech and the puffy face which had stirred rumours that a lifetime of heavy drinking was taking its toll.

But the image of the Yeltsin who climbed on a tank in August 1991 to defy a communist-led putsch in Moscow disappeared abruptly just as his goal was in sight late last June. Yeltsin disappeared from the public eye.

One doctor said he may have had a third heart attack and the president finally announced last September 5 that, faced with the prospect of a steady decline, he had decided to have a make-or-break operation.
He returned to the Kremlin on December 23 but pneumonia forced him to go back to hospital from January 8 to 20.

A building engineer by training, Yeltsin bucked authority from early on as party boss in the industrial Urals city of Sverdlovsk, now Yekaterinburg. He was summoned to the capital as Moscow party chief in 1985 by Gorbachev.
He became a non-voting member of the ruling Politburo but his demands for faster reform lost him favour and he was disgraced by Gorbachev in 1987, starting an enduring feud between the two.

But in March 1989 Yeltsin was elected to parliament in the country's first multi-candidate elections. In July 1990, he gambled again and stalked out of the Communist Party, a move which only increased his popularity.
His moral authority slipped in 1993 when he used tanks to crush a bloody rebellion by parliamentary hardliners in Moscow.
In December 1994 he committed what he later acknowledged to be a blunder, sending troops to Chechnya to try to end its drive for independence. Tens of thousands, mostly civilians, died.
The threat of a communist comeback jolted him, prompting a sudden burst of activity for the 1996 election campaign. He is now intent on going down in history as a great reformer.
Boris Nikolayevich Yeltsin was born in a peasant family in the Ural mountains on February 1, 1931. He has a wife, Naina, two daughters and four grandchildren.
